questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: When choosing my study destination, it was crucial for me to go to a country that felt safe and stable, so I could focus fully on both my studies and daily life. At the same time, I wanted a university with a high academic level, where I would be challenged and gain real academic value from the exchange. Finally, the course offering mattered a lot: I specifically looked for a place where I could take advanced courses like Advanced Microeconomics (Mikro 3) and Advanced Macroeconomics (Makro 3) since they are mandatory at economics.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, my study experience in Zurich has been amazing. I’ve made some really good new friends, explored the local culture, and I can genuinely recommend Zurich as an exchange destination. At the same time, the academic level is very high, so it’s important to be prepared for a demanding workload and high expectations—but that is also a big part of what made the experience so valuable.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Upon arrival, there was a lot of information to take in, but much of it was provided in advance. The University of Zurich (UZH) sent many formal documents beforehand, which helped make the practical and administrative side clearer. I didn’t get much information from KU, mostly the approval of courses.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: When I arrived in Zurich, I received helpful support through a general information session where we were given everything we needed to get started, including the student card and practical guidance on topics like insurance and migration/registration requirements. In addition, there was a separate information session specifically for the Faculty of Business, Economics and Informatics, which I would strongly recommend attending as well, since it provides more targeted and relevant information for students in those programs. They held these faculty specific information meetings for every faculty.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Finding off-campus housing was difficult, and it can take a lot of time and effort. My main recommendation is to start looking as early as possible, since the market is competitive and the best options go quickly.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Living off campus is completely fine in Zurich. Public transport - especially the trains - works very well, so it’s easy to commute and get around the city. Even if you don’t live in the dorms, you can still stay socially connected, for example by joining dorm parties and meeting up with friends who live on campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Regarding housing, I found accommodation on my own together with two other exchange students from my semester. All three of us applied for a dorm through the university, but none of us were offered a room, which we were not prepared for. Over the years it has become more common not to get a dorm room at Meierwiesenstrasse, so future exchange students should be aware of this risk and plan accordingly. My main advice is to start looking for housing early – otherwise you may end up spending your summer holiday searching for a place to live, which can be quite stressful. Facebook groups for WG-Zimmer can be useful, but it is important to be careful, as there are many scammers. In the end, we found an apartment through Blueground, and it has been completely fine for our stay.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Course registration at UZH is straightforward, and the system is flexible since you can change courses during the first month.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration process at UZH is quite simple at first: you sign up for your courses online and you can adjust your choices during the first month. However, from the beginning of October you can no longer change courses, so your final selection has to be settled by then. After finalizing your courses, you must complete a Learning Agreement listing the courses you are taking. This document has to be signed in order by me, KU, and then UZH. In my case, the process took a long time because KU could not sign before my final course approvals were uploaded in Mobility Online, and afterwards UZH was relatively slow with their part. Even though the first month is flexible, I would therefore recommend being well prepared and having a clear idea of which courses you want to take before arriving.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The kind of help available was mainly administrative support from KU. In particular, the studievejleder at KU has been amazing throughout the process. Since the course approval office at KU was sometimes slow, the studievejleder was especially helpful when I needed answers quickly, as they were able to follow up and speed up the process.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was very successful in registering for the classes I wanted, as the course registration process at UZH is easy and straightforward.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: My advice to future exchange students is to go in with a clear idea of which courses you would like to take, and to start the course approval process as early as possible. Even though you can adjust your course choices during the first month at UZH, the formal approvals and paperwork can take time, so being prepared early makes the whole registration process much smoother.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, the academic programme at UZH is tough. The level is high, and you really have to put in consistent work and study regularly to keep up. One thing that also stood out to me is the exam format: the exams are handwritten, and they are typically around a 1.5-hour sit-in exam, which requires you to be well prepared and able to work efficiently under time pressure. You will not be able to finish the exams

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of the courses was generally very high. During my exchange I took a mix of courses – three at Master’s level and two at Bachelor’s level – and the workload reflected that. Since most courses are 6 ECTS, you typically need to take five courses in total, which makes for a full schedule.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching style at UZH was quite similar to UCPH in structure, since most courses had both a weekly lecture and an exercise session. However, the exercise sessions worked a bit differently: you are expected to complete the problem sets in advance, because the Teaching Assistant mainly goes through the solutions in class. In that sense, the exercise class often feels more like an additional lecture where the TA presents the full solution methods rather than a session where you work through tasks during class. A very positive difference was that some courses were recorded, which was really helpful, since it gave me the option to rewatch lectures (and exercise sessions) and clarify things afterwards if I was uncertain about parts of the material.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Advanced Macroeconomics (L+E) (Master course at UZH)
Advanced Microeconomics I (L+E) (Master course at UZH)
Behavioral Finance (L +E) (Bachelor course)
Markets, People, Politics (L&E) (Bachelor course)
Advanced Corporate Finance I (L+E) (Master course)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend Advanced Macroeconomics (L+E) and Advanced Microeconomics I (L+E), since they are core/mandatory courses within economics and fit well into an economics study plan. I would also recommend Behavioral Finance (L+E) because I found it genuinely interesting, and the teaching quality was high – the professor was very good, which made the course both engaging and rewarding.
If you are studying economics, they will get two Nobel Prize winners in development economics from Summer 2026. Try their courses.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did not really encounter any major unexpected costs. Most expenses were predictable, but one cost to be aware of is the registration/administrative fee when you register yourself after arrival, which was 55 CHF.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Overall, everyday life in Zurich is simply expensive — it’s widely regarded as one of the most expensive cities in the world to visit and live in, which you notice quickly in day-to-day costs. This was especially noticeable when it came to food: meals at the university are pricey, and groceries can add up quickly. In particular, some vegetables in supermarkets can be surprisingly expensive, so it’s worth keeping an eye on prices and planning your shopping accordingly.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot of cultural, athletic, and social activities were available for students, especially through ASVZ. Through ASVZ you can join almost any kind of sport; some activities are free, while others require a small fee. This is a really nice opportunity because it’s not only a great way to stay active, but also an easy way to meet other exchange students - and even Swiss students as well. Personally, I used ASVZ for tennis, where you sign up based on your level, which made it accessible and well organized.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Attend the Polyball, which takes place at the end of November.
Go to ASVZ sports activities and, if possible, taking language courses. Both are great ways to meet other exchange students in a natural setting, build a social network quickly, and feel more integrated in everyday life in Zurich beyond just the academic environment.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: On weekends or holidays, I would recommend spending time exploring Zurich itself. A boat trip on Lake Zurich is a really nice way to see the city from a different angle, and if you are there around Christmas, the Christmas markets are definitely worth visiting. I would also suggest walking around the old town (Altstadt), visiting the university areas (Law library), and seeing some of the city’s highlights like the Opera House. If the weather is good, take the Polybahn to the Polyterrasse (ETH) and enjoy a beer there.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Adjusting to the local culture was quite easy for me. In many ways, Swiss people are a bit similar to Danes – friendly and polite, but also fairly reserved, so I wouldn’t expect people to automatically reach out first. Once you take the initiative yourself, it becomes much easier to connect and feel comfortable in the local environment.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Local students can be fairly reserved, so my main tip is to be proactive and not take it personally if people don’t reach out first. I would also strongly recommend signing up for a buddy program if it’s available – some buddies are really kind and can help you integrate by introducing you to their friends and inviting you into their social circles, which makes it much easier to meet locals. Otherwise through sports.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I did not find any major cultural differences particularly challenging. Swiss culture felt quite similar to Danish culture, and it was easy to adapt overall.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: What I appreciated most about Swiss culture was the combination of amazing nature and a society that is extremely well organized. The outdoor opportunities are incredible. You can go hiking or even go skiing simply by taking the train, which makes it very easy to be active on weekends. At the same time, the infrastructure works really well: the train and tram system is efficient and reliable, and it feels like you can get everywhere quickly and smoothly.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Start housing early and be prepared not to get a dorm. Many students don’t get a room through UZH (e.g., Meierwiesenstrasse), so begin looking well in advance and be careful with scams in Facebook WG groups.

2. Be prepared for a high academic level and a different exam format. The courses are demanding, and many exams are handwritten, sit-in exams (often around 1.5 hours), so you need to study consistently and not rely on last-minute preparation.

3. Plan your courses and approvals early, but use the first month wisely. Course registration is easy and you can change courses during the first month, but the Learning Agreement and approvals can take time—so come with a clear idea of what you want to take and start the approval process early to avoid stress.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be aware that Zurich is expensive, so budgeting matters – especially for food – and having a plan for housing and course approvals early can save a lot of stress.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was meeting Swiss people and getting to know locals beyond the exchange community. Building those connections made the stay feel much more authentic and helped me understand Swiss culture and everyday life in a way you don’t get as a tourist.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The greatest challenge during my exchange was studying for the exams. The academic level at UZH is very high, and preparing for the exam period was the toughest part of the entire exchange experience.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I think that’s it - overall I’ve been really happy with the exchange and would definitely recommend Zurich

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
